claim: Photinus carolinus fireflies flash with no intrinsic period between successive bursts when isolated from their peers.
source: In isolation from their peers, Photinus carolinus fireflies flash with no intrinsic period between successive bursts.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations described in the Results section showing irregular interburst intervals for isolated fireflies.

claim: When congregating into large mating swarms, P. carolinus fireflies transition into predictability, synchronizing with their neighbors with a rhythmic periodicity.
source: Yet, when congregating into large mating swarms, these fireflies transition into predictability, synchronizing with their neighbors with a rhythmic periodicity.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing periodic flashing in swarms.

claim: Analytic predictions from the proposed theoretical framework agree strikingly well with experimental data with no fitting parameters.
source: Remarkably, with no fitting parameters, analytic predictions from this simple principle and framework agree strikingly well with data.
evidence: The manuscript presents comparisons between theoretical predictions and experimental data in Figure 3, demonstrating agreement without fitting parameters.

claim: The agent-based computational framework shows quantitatively similar phenomenology to experimental observations.
source: This agent-based framework of P. carolinus fireflies interacting in swarms of increasing density also shows quantitatively similar phenomenology and reduces to the analytic framework in the appropriate limit of the tunable coupling strength.
evidence: The manuscript presents simulation results that match experimental data with fitted beta values, as shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: The resulting dynamics follow the style of a decentralized follow-the-leader synchronization, where any of the randomly flashing individuals may take the role of the leader of any subsequent synchronized flash burst.
source: We discuss our findings and note that the resulting dynamics follow the style of a decentralized follow-the-leader synchronization, where any of the randomly flashing individuals may take the role of the leader of any subsequent synchronized flash burst.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mechanism proposed in the theoretical framework.

claim: In their natural habitat, P. carolinus fireflies produce periodic bursts of flashes occurring with great regularity, with a temperature-dependent period generally around 12 s.
source: Indeed, in their natural habitat, these fireflies produce periodic bursts of flashes occurring with great regularity, with a temperature-dependent period generally around 12 s (Faust, 2010; Moiseff and Copeland, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: When put in isolation, a single P. carolinus firefly does not appear to show any regularity about when it emits its flash trains.
source: Surprisingly, when put in isolation, a single firefly does not appear to show any regularity about when it emits its flash trains (Sarfati et al., 2020), where intervals between flash trains vary between a few seconds to a few minutes apart.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Sarfati et al., 2020 and data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Synchronization is traditionally thought of as the adjustment of rhythms of self-sustained oscillators due to coupling.
source: Synchronization is traditionally thought of as the adjustment of rhythms of self-sustained oscillators due to coupling (Mirollo and Strogatz, 1990; Strogatz, 1997; Strogatz, 2000; Pikovsky et al., 2001; Ramírez Ávila et al., 2003; Ramírez Ávila et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about established scientific understanding supported by multiple citations.

claim: The Kuramoto model and other traditional models addressing synchrony model individuals as oscillators firing highly regularly in isolation, often with different periods.
source: The Kuramoto model and other such traditional models addressing synchrony in systems such as Pteroptyx malaccae fireflies model individuals as oscillators firing highly regularly in isolation, often with different periods.
evidence: This is a characterization of existing models based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Traditional models of limit-cycle oscillators are fundamentally different from the problem posed by the P. carolinus system.
source: This is fundamentally different from the problem posed by our system, in which the individuals, which fire highly irregularly, seem to use synchrony through coupling with other individuals as a tool to achieve greater regularity in their firing period.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the characteristics of P. carolinus with traditional models.

claim: A P. carolinus lek in its natural habitat contains several thousands of fireflies of which the males display a robust collective flash pattern.
source: A P. carolinus lek in its natural habitat contains several thousands of fireflies of which the males display a robust collective flash pattern.
evidence: This is an observational statement about natural P. carolinus behavior.

claim: Collective bursts in the natural swarm have a well-defined period (peak-to-peak) of about 12 s.
source: Collective bursts in the swarm have a well-defined period (peak-to-peak) of about 12 s (Sarfati et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from a previous study.

claim: When a single P. carolinus firefly is taken out of the lek and placed in a large (2 m³) enclosing volume visually insulated from the rest of the group, all periodicity in the occurrence of flash trains is lost.
source: Crucially, however, when a single firefly is taken out of the lek and placed in a large (2 m3) enclosing volume visually insulated from the rest of the group, all periodicity in the occurrence of flash trains is lost.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: The time between successive flash bursts for an isolated firefly varies between a few seconds and a few minutes.
source: The single firefly continues to emit sporadic bursts (Figure 1B and C), but the time between successive flash bursts varies between a few seconds and a few minutes (Figure 1B and Sarfati et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and cited from Sarfati et al., 2020.

claim: Individual interburst intervals (IBIs) for isolated P. carolinus fireflies occur at random.
source: This suggests that individual interburst intervals (IBIs) occur at random, and may thus depend on a variety of behavioral factors.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed variability in interburst intervals.

claim: As the number of fireflies within the enclosing volume is increased, a regularity in the time between bursts starts to emerge.
source: Interestingly, as the number of fireflies within the enclosing volume is increased, a regularity in the time between bursts starts to emerge.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations with varying numbers of fireflies.

claim: Upon flashing, a firefly instantly triggers all other fireflies to also flash.
source: (2) Upon flashing, a firefly instantly triggers all other fireflies to also flash.
evidence: This is a proposed principle of the theoretical framework.

claim: The shortest possible interburst interval is the only one that occurs in large, fully connected, and instantaneously stimulated groups of fireflies.
source: The theoretical predictions are consistent with the intuitive result that the shortest possible interburst interval is the only one that occurs in large, fully connected, and instantaneously stimulated groups of fireflies.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the theoretical predictions.

claim: A threshold minimum time exists owing to physiological constraints, which prevent the fireflies from flashing continuously forever without pause.
source: We expect such a threshold minimum time to exist owing to physiological constraints, which prevent the fireflies from flashing continuously forever without pause.
evidence: This is a speculation based on biological reasoning.

claim: As the number of fireflies increases, there is a greater probability that at least one of those fireflies will flash at an interval close to the minimum.
source: Intuitively, as the number of fireflies increases, there is a greater probability that at least one of those fireflies will flash at an interval close to the minimum.
evidence: This is an intuitive explanation of the mathematical framework.

claim: For any input distribution shape, emergent periodicity and synchrony are guaranteed through the proposed mechanism.
source: Taken together, what these predictions show is that for any input distribution shape, we are guaranteed to get emergent periodicity and synchrony through the proposed mechanism.
evidence: This is a general conclusion from the theoretical analysis.

claim: Attempts at agent-based simulation using extant models such as Kuramoto or integrate-and-fire without incorporation of the insights offered by the theory principle fail to reproduce the basic phenomenology observed in data.
source: At the outset, we clarify that our attempts at agent-based simulation, which simply tweak extant models, such as Kuramoto or integrate-and-fire (IF), without incorporation of the insights offered by the theory principle, framework, and predictions, fail to reproduce the basic phenomenology observed in data.
evidence: This is a statement about unsuccessful modeling attempts.

claim: The computational approach relaxes the assumption that all fireflies immediately start flashing upon seeing any other one flash.
source: In particular, we now relax the assumption that all fireflies immediately start flashing upon seeing any other one flash, since in practice there could be some time delay or imperfect information transfer, which could be made shorter if the firefly sees additional fireflies flashing too.
evidence: This describes a modification to the theoretical framework in the computational approach.

claim: Incorporating the theoretical framework is essential to give rise to emergent periodicity despite having non-oscillating individuals.
source: Thus, incorporating the theoretical framework built up in previous sections is essential to give rise to emergent periodicity despite having non-oscillating individuals.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the necessity of the theoretical framework for the computational approach.

claim: The simulation exhibits a transition to group periodicity as interactions between agents are increased.
source: This simulation exhibits a transition to group periodicity as interactions between agents are increased.
evidence: This is an observation from the computational simulations.

claim: When one firefly flashes in the high coupling regime, it quickly triggers all others.
source: In these regimes, when one firefly flashes, it quickly triggers all others.
evidence: This describes the behavior in the high coupling regime of the simulation.

claim: The optimal β value corresponds with the transition point in the location of the mode of the distributions.
source: This also corresponds with the transition point in the location of the mode of the distributions, as can be seen in Figure 5F.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing fitted β values with distribution modes in Figure 5F.

claim: In P. frontalis fireflies, individuals are intrinsically oscillatory.
source: In other, more commonly studied firefly species such as the P. frontalis, individuals are intrinsically oscillatory (Moiseff and Copeland, 2000), and thus can be modeled by traditional Kuramoto-like models which do not apply to species like ours.
evidence: This is a statement about another firefly species supported by a citation.

claim: Traditional Kuramoto-like models can be used to model P. frontalis but do not apply to P. carolinus.
source: In other, more commonly studied firefly species such as the P. frontalis, individuals are intrinsically oscillatory (Moiseff and Copeland, 2000), and thus can be modeled by traditional Kuramoto-like models which do not apply to species like ours.
evidence: This is a comparison between modeling approaches for different species.

claim: A model based on the concept of elliptic bursters has been successful at producing many aspects of P. carolinus' collective flashing, notably the intermittent (burst-type) synchrony.
source: More recently, a new model based on the concept of elliptic bursters has been successful at producing many aspects of P. carolinus' collective flashing, notably the intermittent (burst-type) synchrony.
evidence: This is a statement about another modeling approach.

claim: The elliptic burster model still assumes intrinsic periodicity between flash bursts.
source: Yet, this model still assumes intrinsic periodicity between flash bursts (McCrea et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a critique of another model supported by a citation.

claim: All the input parameters for application of the framework and the computational approach come directly from experimental results.
source: All the input parameters for application of the framework as well as the computational approach come directly from experimental results in Sarfati et al., 2020 and subsequent field season results from the Great Smoky Mountains: the wide distribution of interburst intervals for single isolated fireflies, the two timescales required by the computational approach of charging time and discharging time are both data-driven from Sarfati et al., 2020.
evidence: This describes the data sources for model parameters.

claim: The fitting curve is flat, implying that several beta values could possibly achieve a satisfactory fit.
source: While we do not currently have an explanation for why the fitted parameter values are what they are, we note that the fitting curve is flat, implying that several beta values could possibly achieve a satisfactory fit.
evidence: This is an observation about the parameter fitting landscape.

claim: If the number of fireflies increases indefinitely, or if there are visual obstacles in the environment, the assumption that each firefly can practically immediately perceive when another firefly starts flashing will no longer hold.
source: If the number of fireflies increases indefinitely, or if there are visual obstacles in the environment, the assumption that each firefly can practically immediately perceive when another firefly starts flashing will no longer hold.
evidence: This is a speculation about limitations of the model.

claim: A finite time delay in perceiving the onset of the flashing could lead to an interburst interval that is greater than what is expected for the ideal case.
source: In this case, a finite time delay in perceiving the onset of the flashing could lead to an interburst interval that is greater than what is expected for the ideal case.
evidence: This is a speculation about the effect of time delays.

claim: Existing mathematical models on synchronous periodic behavior generally consider individuals to be intrinsically oscillatory.
source: Existing mathematical models on synchronous periodic behavior generally consider individuals to be intrinsically oscillatory, which either oscillate periodically in isolation or have their oscillations suppressed at low numbers through a sufficiently strong coupling with the environment.
evidence: This is a characterization of existing models based on scientific knowledge.

claim: In the proposed framework, individuals that are intrinsically non-oscillatory make use of the synchronization through coupling with other individuals to produce emergent oscillatory behavior.
source: Conversely, in our proposed framework, individuals that are intrinsically non-oscillatory make use of the synchronization through coupling with other individuals to produce emergent oscillatory behavior, which becomes more regular as more individuals are added.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the proposed framework.

claim: Systems of oscillators interacting with Kuramoto-style mean field and limit cycle oscillators tend to converge on the mean frequency of the heterogeneous group.
source: For example, systems of oscillators interacting with Kuramoto-style mean field and limit cycle oscillators such as those used in dynamical quorum sensing models tend to converge on the mean frequency of the heterogeneous group (Pikovsky et al., 2001; De Monte et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about existing models supported by citations.

claim: Observations of the P. carolinus fireflies show convergence on the fastest frequency in the repertoire of isolated individual fireflies.
source: However, observations of the P. carolinus fireflies show convergence on the fastest frequency in the repertoire of isolated individual fireflies and a synchronization of relaxation periods also seen in some coupled IF units (Bottani, 1996) which have been applied to many biological systems such as the synchronization of pacemaker cells in the mammalian heart (Jongsma et al., 1983; Jalife and Michaels, 1989).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: In typical coupled IF units, the 'fastest frequency' is the frequency of the individual oscillator with the fastest frequency.
source: In typical coupled IF units, this is the frequency of the individual oscillator with the fastest frequency.
evidence: This is a statement about typical IF models based on scientific knowledge.

claim: In the P. carolinus system, the individuals fire sporadically, thus there is no specific frequency associated with any individual.
source: But in our system, the individuals fire sporadically, thus there is no specific frequency associated with any individual.
evidence: This is an observation about P. carolinus behavior.

claim: The 'fastest frequency' in the P. carolinus system is an emergent phenomenon in large groups, formed from the collective minimum interburst intervals of the individuals.
source: Instead, the 'fastest frequency' is an emergent phenomenon in large groups, formed from the collective minimum interburst intervals of the individuals.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mechanism in P. carolinus.

claim: In the limit of an infinitely large and entirely connected swarm, the smallest IBI always occurs.
source: That means that in the limit of an infinitely large and entirely connected swarm, the smallest IBI always occurs.
evidence: This is a consequence of the mathematical framework.

claim: While most of the smallest IBI from an isolated firefly peak at 12 s and more, there are some residual values between 5 s and 12 s.
source: This is at odds with two empirical observations: (1) while most of the smallest IBI from an isolated firefly peak at 12 s and more, there are some residual values between 5 s and 12 s
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: Natural swarms comprising thousands of fireflies do not exhibit a 5 s period.
source: (2) natural swarms comprising thousands of fireflies do not exhibit a 5 s period.
evidence: This is an observation from natural swarms.

claim: It is possible that isolated fireflies in a confining volume switch to different behavioral modes that produce atypical flash trains with intervals less than what they would typically do in an unobstructed environment with responding peers.
source: It is possible that isolated fireflies in a confining volume switch to different behavioral modes that produce atypical flash trains with intervals less than what they would typically do in an unobstructed environment with responding peers.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain discrepancies between model and observations.

claim: Fireflies are known to produce annex flash patterns, for instance, for alarm, in addition to the primary courtship phase.
source: First, fireflies are known to produce annex flash patterns, for instance, for alarm, in addition to the primary courtship phase.
evidence: This is a statement about firefly behavior based on general knowledge.

claim: It is possible that the swarm buffers against unusual perturbations.
source: Secondly, it is possible that the swarm buffers against unusual perturbations.
evidence: This is a speculation about swarm behavior.

claim: The swarm is not all-to-all connected.
source: More than finite-size effects, the main caveat here is that the swarm is not all-to-all connected, as we showed previously (Sarfati et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about swarm structure supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: If the swarm is not all-to-all connected, the dynamics of the system would depend upon the speed of propagation of information across the swarm.
source: In this case, the dynamics of the system would depend upon the speed of propagation of information across the swarm.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of limited connectivity.

claim: Artificial flash entrainment with an LED should be able to decrease the inter-burst interval.
source: A promising avenue consists of artificially and controllably tuning the interactions within the group, for example, artificial flash entrainment with an LED should be able to decrease the inter-burst interval.
evidence: This is a speculation about future experiments.

claim: The individual and collective flashing of P. carolinus fireflies was recorded during 10 nights of field experiments in June 2020 in Great Smoky Mountains National Park (Tennessee, USA).
source: The individual and collective flashing of P. carolinus fireflies was recorded during 10 nights of field experiments in June 2020 in Great Smoky Mountains National Park (Tennessee, USA).
evidence: This describes the experimental data collection.

claim: Individual fireflies in visual isolation do not exhibit burst periodicity.
source: However, it has been observed previously that individual fireflies in visual isolation do not exhibit burst periodicity.
evidence: This is a statement about previous observations.

claim: A GoPro Fusion 360° camera placed inside the tent recorded the entire volume at 30 or 60 frames-per-second (fps).
source: A GoPro Fusion 360° camera placed inside the tent recorded the entire volume at 30 or 60 frames-per-second (fps).
evidence: This describes the experimental recording method.

claim: Flashes were detected in video processing by intensity thresholding.
source: Flashes were detected in video processing by intensity thresholding.
evidence: This describes the data analysis method.

claim: Bursts were identified as (temporal) connected components of flashes less than 2 s apart.
source: Bursts were identified as (temporal) connected components of flashes less than 2 s apart.
evidence: This describes the data analysis method.

claim: 10 individual fireflies were observed alone in the tent, over durations between 5 min and 85 min.
source: We observed 10 individual fireflies alone in the tent, over durations between 5 min and 85 min.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Although isolated fireflies produced flash trains at a frequency of about 2 Hz, the delay between successive trains was apparently randomly distributed, from a few seconds to tens of minutes.
source: We observed that although these fireflies produced flash trains at a frequency of about 2 Hz, the delay between successive trains was apparently randomly distributed, from a few seconds to tens of minutes.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: Three sets of experiments were carried out with 5, 10, 15, and 20 fireflies, using the segments between 9 min and 15 min.
source: Then, we carried out three sets of experiments with 5, 10, 15, and 20 fireflies, using the segments between 9 min and 15 min.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Collective burst flashing only appears at about 15 fireflies.
source: As previously reported, collective burst flashing only appears at about 15 fireflies.
evidence: This is a statement about previous observations.

claim: After the paper's acceptance, a small subset of data points was updated.
source: After the paper's acceptance, a small subset of data points was updated for the reasons described in the correction notice (Sarfati et al., 2025).
evidence: This is a statement about data corrections.

claim: All analyses were repeated after data correction and the findings are unaffected.
source: We repeated all analyses and confirmed that the findings are unaffected.
evidence: This is a statement about the robustness of the results.

claim: Both the original and corrected datasets are publicly available.
source: Both the original and corrected datasets are publicly available.
evidence: This is a statement about data availability.

claim: For each set of parameters, simulations were run for thirty trials of 200,000 timesteps each.
source: For each set of parameters, we ran simulations for thirty trials of 200,000 timesteps each.
evidence: This describes the simulation protocol.
